questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: An intubated patient has an air leak from an intact, cuffed ETT whose cuff is simply under-inflated. What is the appropriate action?
options: Exchange the tube over a bougie
questions.explanation: Inadequate cuff inflation that can be corrected by increasing cuff pressure is a contraindication to tube exchange; exchange is reserved for a damaged or uncuffed tube causing a significant leak.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: Which device is used to view the glottic opening during an endotracheal tube exchange?
questions.explanation: Laryngoscopy is performed with the video laryngoscope to identify the original tube with the bougie in the glottic opening; the exchange must always be done under visualization.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: Before the bougie is passed during an endotracheal tube exchange, how is the existing tube's securement handled?
options: Operator holds the ETT; assistant removes the securement
Assistant holds the ETT; operator removes the securement
Securement stays on until the cuff is deflated
Securement is cut after the bougie is placed
questions.explanation: The operator holds the ETT while the assistant removes the device or tape, so the tube cannot migrate before the assistant advances the bougie through it.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: During an endotracheal tube exchange, hold-up is felt while the bougie is being advanced through the existing tube. What should be done?
options: Advance until the carina is felt
Rotate the bougie and keep advancing
questions.explanation: Advancement stops if hold-up is met; the bougie should sit at the mid-trachea markings and never be pushed deeper, then be held in that position for the rest of the procedure.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: During an endotracheal tube exchange, who loads the new tube onto the bougie and advances it to the patient's mouth?
options: Whichever crew member holds the laryngoscope
Neither; it is pre-loaded before laryngoscopy
questions.explanation: Once the old tube is off, the assistant loads the new ETT and advances it until it reaches the mouth with the bougie protruding from its proximal end; the assistant then takes the bougie while the operator takes and advances the ETT.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: What medications should be given in preparation for an endotracheal tube exchange?
questions.explanation: Additional sedation and paralytic agents should be administered (per RSI) — the exchange is meant to mirror a standard intubation as closely as possible.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: During an endotracheal tube exchange, for how long must the view of the glottic opening be maintained?
options: Until the new tube is in place
Until the old tube clears the cords
questions.explanation: The glottic view is held throughout until the new tube is in place — losing it while only a bougie is in the trachea risks loss of the airway.

questions.title: Endotracheal Tube Exchange
questions.stem: An endotracheal tube exchange starts to go badly. What approach should guide the crew's response?
options: The usual principles of airway management
Continue advancing blind over the bougie
questions.explanation: The procedure is kept as similar as possible to standard intubation precisely so that when things go sideways the usual airway management principles apply; it must never be done blind.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Besides hypoxia, which blood gas derangement is an indication for high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia, hypercarbia, mild-to-moderate respiratory distress and pre/apneic oxygenation for RSI are the indications; the high flow washes out excess CO2 as well as raising delivered O2.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which patient has a contraindication to high flow nasal cannula?
options: A hypercarbic patient in mild distress
A patient in moderate respiratory distress
questions.explanation: Epistaxis is a contraindication, along with basilar skull fracture, recent nose/oropharynx/esophageal surgery and nasal obstruction; the other three are indications.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: On high flow nasal cannula, what are the flow rate and FiO2 each titrated to?
options: Flow to oxygenation; FiO2 to work of breathing
Flow to ETCO2; FiO2 to work of breathing
Flow to work of breathing; FiO2 to oxygenation
questions.explanation: Flow is titrated to work of breathing and FiO2 to oxygenation needs — the two settings treat different problems.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What oral intake instruction applies to a patient placed on high flow nasal cannula for transport?
questions.explanation: The procedure directs keeping the patient NPO, even though in hospital HFNC is often used partly because it lets patients eat and drink.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which RAM cannula is suggested for a 900 g preemie on high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: The sizing guide lists green for < 1 kg (preemie); white is only for < 750 g micro preemies. The sizing card carried with the cannulas takes precedence.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which RAM cannula is suggested for a 2 kg newborn on high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Blue covers 1 - 2.5 kg (newborn) on the sizing guide; prongs must still not occlude more than 80% of the nares.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which RAM cannula is suggested for a 4 kg infant on high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Orange is listed for > 2.5 kg (infant). The guide does not supersede the sizing card carried with the cannulas.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: A hospitalized patient on high flow nasal cannula needs only low-end flows. What may they tolerate for transport instead?
questions.explanation: HFNC is often a convenience in hospital; low-flow patients may tolerate a NRB for transport, while those with higher flow requirements may do better on CPAP or BiPAP.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: How does high flow nasal cannula help a patient with excess CO2?
options: Flow beyond what the patient ventilates displaces CO2
It increases the patient's respiratory rate
It stimulates the central respiratory drive
It adds a mandatory tidal volume to each breath
questions.explanation: High flow delivers gas volumes beyond the patient's own ventilation, displacing excess CO2 while increasing delivered O2.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What is the trade-off of running a RAM cannula from regular oxygen tubing on a flow meter instead of the Hamilton T-1?
options: Higher flow but no FiO2 control
No change if the flow meter is set to 15 LPM
Lower maximum flow and no humidification
Loss of oxygen-conserving LPO mode only
questions.explanation: The 'Christmas tree' method is permitted when the T-1 isn't available, but it results in a reduced maximum flow rate and lack of humidification.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for a 3.5 kg neonate?
questions.explanation: Size 1 (neonate) covers 2–5 kg (5–11 lbs); size 1.5 starts at 5 kg.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for an infant weighing 18 lbs?
questions.explanation: Size 1.5 (infant) covers 11–25 lbs; size 1 tops out at 11 lbs and size 2 starts at 22 lbs.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for an 18 kg child?
questions.explanation: Size 2 (small pediatric) covers 10–25 kg; 2.5 begins at 25 kg.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for a child weighing 60 lbs?
questions.explanation: Size 2.5 (large pediatric) covers 55–77 lbs (25–35 kg); size 2 stops at 55 lbs.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for a small-framed adult weighing 40 kg?
questions.explanation: Size 3 (small adult) covers 30–60 kg; size 4 starts at 50 kg and 2.5 ends at 35 kg.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for an adult weighing 150 lbs?
questions.explanation: Size 4 (medium adult) covers 110–200 lbs (50–90 kg); size 3 tops out at 130 lbs and size 5 is for 200+ lbs.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is used for a large adult weighing 110 kg?
questions.explanation: Size 5 (large adult) is for 90+ kg (200+ lbs); size 4 covers 50–90 kg.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: What weight range is the size 2.5 i-gel intended for?
questions.explanation: Size 2.5 is the large pediatric device, 25–35 kg (55–77 lbs), bridging size 2 (10–25 kg) and size 3 (30–60 kg).

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: What weight range is the size 4 i-gel intended for?
questions.explanation: Size 4 is the medium adult device, 50–90 kg (110–200 lbs); above 90 kg use size 5.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: What color identifies the size 4 (medium adult) i-gel?
questions.explanation: Size 4 is green; size 3 is yellow, size 5 orange and size 2 grey.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: You pull an orange i-gel from the airway kit. Which size is it?
questions.explanation: Orange is size 5, the large adult device for 90+ kg; green is 4, yellow 3, grey 2.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: How far is the i-gel glided down and back along the hard palate during insertion?
options: Until the cuff passes the teeth
Until the patient begins to gag
Until a definitive resistance is felt
questions.explanation: A continuous, gentle push continues until a definitive resistance is felt, without excessive force; at that point the tip should sit in the upper esophageal opening.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: When an i-gel is correctly seated, where should the patient's incisors rest?
questions.explanation: Correct position has the tip in the upper esophageal opening, the cuff against the laryngeal framework and the incisors resting on the integral bite block.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: An unconscious patient with no gag reflex is known to have swallowed drain cleaner. Is an i-gel appropriate?
options: Yes — an absent gag makes it indicated
Yes, if a gastric tube is passed
Yes, one size smaller than weight suggests
questions.explanation: Caustic ingestion is a listed contraindication even though the patient otherwise meets the indication (unconscious, respiratory compromise, absent gag).

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: In an adult whose tibial tuberosity cannot be palpated, where is the proximal tibia IO insertion site?
options: About 1-2 cm below the patella and 1 cm medial
About 3 cm below the inferior border of the patella
About 1-2 cm above the superior border of the patella
About 3 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: Without a palpable tuberosity, go about 3 cm below the inferior patellar border, on the same line the site would be if the tuberosity were felt (normally ~2 cm medial to it). 1-2 cm below and 1 cm medial is the pediatric figure.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Which bony landmark is palpated on the anterior shoulder to locate the proximal humerus IO site?
questions.explanation: With the arm adducted and internally rotated, the greater tubercle is palpated by letting it sink into the palm of your hand.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: For a proximal humerus IO, the arm is placed tight against the body. How is the hand positioned?
options: Palm facing forward, thumb pointing up
Palm facing inward, thumb pointing up
Palm facing outward, thumb pointing down
Palm up, resting on the thigh
questions.explanation: Adduct and internally rotate: arm tight to the body with palm outward and thumb down, or the hand placed over the abdomen with the arm tight against the body.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: How do you make sure an adult distal tibia IO site is mid-line on the bone?
options: Palpate the anterior and posterior borders of the tibia
Palpate the medial and lateral malleoli
Palpate the head of the fibula
questions.explanation: The site is about 3 cm proximal to the most prominent part of the medial malleolus; the anterior and posterior tibial borders are palpated so the needle goes into the flat center of the bone.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: In a child whose tibial tuberosity can be palpated, where is the proximal tibia IO insertion site?
options: About 2 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity
About 3 cm below the inferior border of the patella
About 1 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity
About 1-2 cm above the superior border of the patella
questions.explanation: Pediatric proximal tibia is about 1 cm medial to the tuberosity; 2 cm medial is the adult figure and 1-2 cm above the patella is the pediatric distal femur.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: In a child whose tibial tuberosity cannot be palpated, where is the proximal tibia IO insertion site?
options: About 1-2 cm below the patella and about 1 cm medial
About 3 cm below the inferior border of the patella
About 1-2 cm above the patella and 1 cm medial
About 2 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity
questions.explanation: Without a palpable tuberosity in a child, go about 1-2 cm below the patella and about 1 cm medial on the flat aspect of the tibia; 3 cm below the patella is the adult figure.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Where is the pediatric distal tibia IO insertion site?
options: About 3 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
About 1 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity
About 1-2 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
About 1-2 cm proximal to the patella
questions.explanation: In children the distal tibia site is about 1-2 cm proximal to the most prominent aspect of the medial malleolus (3 cm in adults), on the flat center of the bone.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: How is the leg positioned for a pediatric distal femur IO?
options: Knee flexed to 90 degrees over a roll
Hip externally rotated, knee slightly bent
Outstretched and secured so the knee cannot bend
Knee flexed with the foot flat on the stretcher
questions.explanation: The site is secured with the leg outstretched so the knee does not bend, then located 1-2 cm proximal to the superior patella and about 1 cm medial to mid-line.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Which IO insertion site usually has the least overlying soft tissue?
questions.explanation: Palpation estimates tissue depth for needle choice: the humeral head and femoral sites typically have more overlying tissue than the proximal tibia, and the distal tibia usually has the least.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: With the IO needle tip on the bone, the 5-mm mark is not visible above the skin. What should be done?
options: Drill anyway and accept the depth
Push harder before squeezing the trigger
Withdraw slightly and re-angle the needle
Use a longer needle and/or another insertion site
questions.explanation: If the 5-mm mark (the most proximal mark to the hub) is not visible, the needle is too short for the tissue depth; choose a longer needle and/or a different site to ensure adequate placement depth.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: At what angle is the IO needle pushed through the skin to rest on the bone?
options: Angled toward the foot, away from the joint
Parallel to the long axis of the bone
questions.explanation: The needle is held at 90 degrees to the bone and pushed through the skin until it rests on bone before the trigger is squeezed.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: A patient with a left total knee replacement needs IO access. Which site must be avoided?
questions.explanation: A prosthetic implant at the insertion site is a contraindication; the other limbs remain available (recent IO in the same limb within 24 hours and fracture of the bone are the other contraindications).

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Why must a newly placed IO be flushed rapidly before fluids are infused?
options: To dilute the lidocaine in the space
To test the extension set for leaks
To clear air from the stylet tract
questions.explanation: A rapid flush displaces marrow from the medullary space and also confirms placement; patency is confirmed again before medications or fluids.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Which IO patient should be considered for 2% lidocaine before infusion?
options: A patient who is responsive to pain
questions.explanation: Lidocaine is carried 'if conscious' and analgesia is recommended for patients responsive to pain, because IO infusion under pressure is painful.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What initial dose of 2% lidocaine is given for IO pain management in a 24 kg child?
questions.explanation: Pediatric initial dose is 0.5 mg/kg (max 40 mg): 0.5 × 24 = 12 mg, below the cap. 6 mg would be the half-dose repeat.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: An adult remains in pain after the initial IO lidocaine dose. How much 2% lidocaine is given as the repeat dose?
questions.explanation: The repeat is HALF the initial dose: the adult initial dose is 40 mg, so 20 mg, infused over 60 seconds.
